summary: The two board-specific custom blocks are built the way the hardware is built. The math box is a microcoded bit-slice processor. It reads 24-bit microwords from six 4-bit PROMs, starts at an entry point taken from a command PROM, and runs an Am2901-style ALU. MAME instead hand-codes each command as a C algorithm. The AVG is driven by the original 256x4 state PROM, with normalization and binary scaling done as shift-register and timer-chain operations. The CPU glue logic and memory map are neutral, and the video/framebuffer path is MiSTer presentation code.

findings.signal: Math box executes original microcode PROMs
findings.note: The microword is assembled from six 4-bit PROMs (prom_e1..prom_l1), indexed by a micro_pc that is loaded from a 32-entry command PROM on start. MAME's go_w is a switch over command offsets, with hand-written multiply/divide/window/distance algorithms and no microcode at all.

The code has an R/S source select (AQ,AB,ZQ,ZB,ZA,DA,DQ,DZ), eight ALU functions with carry/overflow, and destination codes with RAM/Q up/down shifts. That is the 2901 slice instruction set, a different decomposition from MAME's per-command int32 arithmetic.

The high and low byte slices get separate I2 bits, a multiply bit flips I1 based on the previous Q0, a jump is gated by the shifted MSB, and a stall bit drops busy. These are board wiring details of the math box, not of any software algorithm.

findings.signal: AVG sequencer driven by state PROM with feedback
findings.note: The PROM address is {running, opcode, previous PROM output}, and output bit 3 selects one of eight latch/strobe actions (LATCH0-3, STROBE0-3) that the code then dispatches. The sequencing comes from the loaded 136002-125 contents, not from a hard-coded per-opcode routine. avgdvg.cpp was not in the comparison set, so I could not check how closely MAME's AVG shares this shape.

findings.signal: Normalization/scaling as shift registers plus timer chain
findings.note: DVX/DVY shift left one bit per master clock until the top two bits differ, while a 15-bit timer shifts right with a 1 filled in at the top. An 8-bit SVEC sub-timer boundary and a binary-scale down-count do further fill shifts. Draw duration therefore comes from a counter-chain value rather than a computed length.

findings.signal: LATCH1 partial clears of operand latches
findings.note: Loading the opcode byte clears DVY0-7, DVX0-12 and the Z modifier bits, but not DVY8-12. That is per-latch-chip clear behaviour a software emulator has no reason to reproduce.

findings.signal: AVG fetches in hardware latch byte order
findings.note: The AVG fetch address inverts A0 so the high byte (opcode) is latched first, and the AVG waits for its own tagged read on the shared vector-memory port. This follows the board's latch order rather than a 16-bit word read.

findings.signal: IRQ from counter chain cleared by WDCLR
findings.note: IRQ is asserted when a 4-bit counter of 3 kHz ticks reaches bits 3 and 2 set, and the counter stops there until a write to 5000 clears it. That is a counter/decoder implementation where MAME uses a periodic-interrupt callback; the rate is the same.

The decode compares exact addresses (4000, 4800, 5000, 5800, 6040...) that match MAME's main_map one for one, with no board-style partial decoding or mirroring. Under the rubric a memory map is shared ground, so this counts at most as a very slight MAME-ward hint.
Bit 8 of a 1.5 MHz divide-by-512 counter drives the 3 kHz status bit, and output bit 2 selects player 1 or 2 controls. Both match MAME, but any correct core must share them.
The EAROM decodes control bits 3:1 into erase/write/read and reads on the rising edge of the CK bit, a simplified pin-level model. It has neither MAME's er2055 device structure nor real cell timing.

findings.signal: Digital integrator and MiSTer video path
findings.note: Beam motion is a digital accumulator scaled by the inverted linear scale, and the raster framebuffer, geometry and phosphor pipeline are FPGA presentation code. Both are neutral under the rubric's FPGA-engineering rule.
